title: Ines and the Summer
premise: Ines Fairweather, a single father running the town's only bookshop, has spent a decade hiding behind a quiet, careful life since the night his testimony sent his best friend to prison. When the town's summer festival launches an anonymous pen-pal program, Ines is matched with a correspondent who knows too much—and turns out to be Marisol Vega, the sister of the man he convicted and the new deputy determined to reopen the case. As their anonymous letters deepen into something like love, Marisol uncovers evidence that the conviction was wrong and that Ines has known it for years. Ines must choose between the loyalty that has defined him and the truth he owes everyone, confessing his decade-old silence publicly at the festival's closing night—and winning, tentatively, a second chance with Marisol as the summer ends.
about_author: Astrid Eastwick is the pen name of a former small-town librarian who now writes romance from a converted ferry cabin on the northern coast. Her novels are known for stubborn, bookish protagonists and love stories that arrive exactly one season too late.

chapters.title: The Weight of Quiet Years
chapters.summary: Ines Fairweather opens his bookshop on a gray June morning, navigating school-run chaos with his daughter Wren and the careful routines that keep his past sealed. A letter from the festival committee announces the town's first anonymous pen-pal program. Ines almost declines. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: the ache of a life built to be invisible.

chapters.title: A Stranger's Handwriting
chapters.summary: Ines writes his first guarded letter; the reply that arrives is sharp, funny, and unsettlingly perceptive. Meanwhile, Deputy Marisol Vega arrives in town to take up her post, recognized by Ines with a cold jolt: she is the sister of Daniel Vega, the man he helped convict ten years ago. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: dread disguised as curiosity.

chapters.title: The Deputy's Ledger
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV as she settles in, officially here for the job, unofficially carrying her brother's case files and a decade of her family's grief. She joins the pen-pal program on a whim, writing with a candor she shows no one. She and Ines collide at the bookshop, polite and brittle. Emotional beat: grief sharpened into purpose.

chapters.title: Letters Between Enemies
chapters.summary: The anonymous correspondence deepens: Ines finds himself confessing things he's never written down, and Marisol's correspondent becomes the only place she isn't the deputy. In person, she and Ines spar over a disputed land deed that touches the old Vega property. POV: alternating. Emotional beat: the dangerous comfort of being truly known.

chapters.title: What Wren Remembers
chapters.summary: Ines's daughter Wren, now eleven, innocently mentions memories of 'Uncle Danny,' forcing Ines to confront how much she absorbed of that summer. He deflects, but the cracks show. Marisol, meanwhile, requests her brother's trial records. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: guilt surfacing through a child's eyes.

chapters.title: The Festival Opens
chapters.summary: The summer festival begins—lanterns, a book stall, the whole town out in force. Ines and Marisol are thrown together organizing the literary tent, their friction softening into reluctant teamwork. Their pen-pal letters grow warmer the same week. POV: Marisol. Emotional beat: attraction she refuses to name.

chapters.title: An Inconsistency in the File
chapters.summary: Marisol finds a discrepancy in the trial evidence: a witness statement that was quietly withdrawn. She begins pulling threads. Ines, reading her letter describing 'a case I can't let go of,' realizes with horror who his correspondent might be. POV: Marisol, closing with Ines's panic. Emotional beat: the past knocking at the door.

chapters.title: The Sentence Rehearsed
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter: the night a decade ago when Ines gave his statement—the pressure from the town, from Daniel's own family, and the detail he omitted to protect someone he loved. The chapter reveals the sentence he has rehearsed ever since and never said aloud. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: shame crystallized.

chapters.title: Almost Telling
chapters.summary: Ines drafts a letter to his pen-pal that comes close to confession, then burns it. In person, Marisol asks him directly what he remembers about the Vega case; he lies, and hates how easily it comes. Wren befriends Marisol at the shop. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: cowardice curdling into self-disgust.

chapters.title: The Witness Who Recanted
chapters.summary: Marisol tracks down the withdrawn witness, an old shopkeeper now dying, who hints the statement was changed after a visit from a prominent town family. The trail points somewhere Marisol doesn't want it to go: toward the Fairweather name. POV: Marisol. Emotional beat: hope and dread braided together.

chapters.title: Rain on the Tent Roof
chapters.summary: A storm strands Ines and Marisol in the festival tent after closing. Soaked, laughing, guard down, they nearly kiss—until she mentions the case and he withdraws so abruptly it wounds her. That night both write their pen-pals with raw honesty. POV: alternating. Emotional beat: intimacy interrupted by the secret.

chapters.title: Two Halves of One Truth
chapters.summary: Marisol's correspondent unknowingly describes details only someone connected to the trial could know. She begins cross-checking handwriting from the bookshop's order slips against her letters. Ines, sensing her investigation closing in, considers leaving town with Wren. POV: Marisol. Emotional beat: the hunt turning personal.

chapters.title: Wren's Question
chapters.summary: Wren asks her father why he never talks about Danny Vega, revealing she found an old photograph. Ines tells her a partial truth—that he was there that night and has been afraid ever since. Wren's response is devastatingly simple: 'Are you the bad guy?' POV: Ines. Emotional beat: a child's verdict cutting deeper than any court's.

chapters.title: The Match Revealed
chapters.summary: At the festival's midsummer letter-reading event, the pen-pal identities are meant to be revealed. Ines tries to withdraw; Marisol, having already matched the handwriting, engineers the reveal herself. The town watches as Ines and Marisol stand face to face, both unmasked. POV: Marisol. Emotional beat: betrayal and relief arriving in the same breath.

chapters.title: Everything I Didn't Write
chapters.summary: The confrontation: Marisol demands the truth, Ines finally begins to give it—admitting he saw who tampered with the evidence and stayed silent because the culprit was his late wife's father, the town's beloved judge. Marisol walks out. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: confession without absolution.

chapters.title: The Judge's House
chapters.summary: Marisol investigates the dead judge's records with Ines's reluctant help, finding a sealed letter among his effects—a near-confession, and proof Daniel's conviction rested on doctored evidence. Ines must decide whether to hand it over and destroy his family's name. POV: Marisol. Emotional beat: justice becoming real and costly.

chapters.title: What Loyalty Costs
chapters.summary: Ines's late wife's family, still powerful in town, pressures him to stay silent; Wren's place in school, his lease, his reputation all hang in the balance. An old friend begs him to think of Wren. Ines spends a sleepless night with the letter. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: the last excuse burning away.

chapters.title: The Night Before the Closing
chapters.summary: On the festival's final eve, Ines visits Daniel Vega in prison for the first time in ten years. The meeting is raw—anger, then something like mercy. Daniel tells him the truth was never Ines's to carry alone. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: forgiveness offered before it was earned.

chapters.title: Closing Night
chapters.summary: Before the whole town at the festival's closing ceremony, Ines takes the stage and says the sentence he has rehearsed for a decade: that he lied, that the judge doctored the evidence, that Daniel Vega is innocent. The crowd's silence, then the fallout. Marisol watches from the back, unreadable. POV: Marisol. Emotional beat: the climax—truth as public act.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: The town splits; some doors close to Ines, others open. Daniel's exoneration process begins. Wren takes her father's hand in public, unashamed. Marisol, promoted and conflicted, stays away from the bookshop—until she finds one last letter in her mailbox, unsigned but unmistakably his. POV: Marisol. Emotional beat: grief giving way to something gentler.

chapters.title: The Last Letter
chapters.summary: Ines writes one final pen-pal letter—not anonymous, addressed to Marisol by name—laying out everything he couldn't say on the stage, including that he loves her, and that he expects nothing. He leaves it with the shop open, the festival lights coming down outside. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: hope without demand.

chapters.title: Ines and the Summer
chapters.summary: September arrives. Marisol comes to the bookshop not as a deputy but as herself, and answers his letter in person: slowly, honestly, they begin. Daniel's release date is set; Wren hangs a new photograph on the wall. The summer ends, but the season's promise holds. POV: alternating, closing on both. Emotional beat: a second chance, finally well-timed.
